title: In the 'Field' of Transnational Professionals: A Post-Bourdieusian Approach to Transnational Legal Entrepreneurs
pub: ch. 2 in Leonard Seabrooke & Lasse Folke Henriksen (eds), Professional Networks in Transnational Governance (Cambridge University Press, 2017), pp. 25–38
author: Yves Dezalay · Mikael Rask Madsen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses transnational legal power, professional hierarchies and reflexive research methodology, not legal AI capability, verification, selective deployment or workflow redesign. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Elite renewal: Innovation can reproduce legal power
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of legal authority as relatively autonomous yet embedded in state power and elite reproduction. It materially extends that account to transnational professional competition, showing how mobility, organisational resources and selective internationalisation reproduce privilege, while also developing a reflexive, multi-site research strategy.
qs: Our basic contention is that these processes of professional competition are not simply battles over professional control; they are also part of more general processes of for example elite reproduction of national legal fields and beyond.

More generally, this approach helps to explain and demonstrate the paradox formulated by Kantorowicz: the clerks of the law affirm their autonomy with respect to power at the same time as they put their expertise in the service of power.

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: The source accepts jurisdictional competition as important but materially extends the cluster’s authority-and-power framing by embedding jurisdictional struggles in a broader transnational field and requiring reflexive scrutiny of how scholarship constructs and naturalises its objects. It is conceptual rather than empirical and makes no AI-specific forecast.
qs: While battles over jurisdiction are evidently important also in the Bourdieusian framework, the key difference is in the broader sociological picture that is taken into account when taking the Bourdieusian route.
To take the Bourdieusian perspective seriously this naturally implies interrogating the construction of the object and the naturalizing tendencies of academic discourse on that very object.

kp.k: Professional and organizational resources jointly underpin issue control
kp.d: This historical and theoretical chapter does not discuss AI. Drawing on their research into international commercial arbitration, human rights and environmental law, the authors argue that transnational legal entrepreneurs combine professional and organizational resources. Separating these logics too sharply risks obscuring how actors create categories and institutions to control transnational issues.
qs: one of the central characteristics of professional ‘strategies of internationalization’ is that they combine professional and organizational resources.
the boundaries between professional and institutional logics often are blurred – and tacitly so.

kp.k: National stratification shapes international professional alliances
kp.d: The authors argue that internationalization must be explained through national legal hierarchies and the constraints and opportunities they generate. Citing Sacriste and Vauchez, they illustrate this with early twentieth-century international institutionalized law: business lawyers seeking roles as statesmen and philanthropists converged with marginalized international-law professors seeking diplomatic influence.
qs: the forms of stratification inscribed in and reproduced by the national legal fields

This process was helped by the convergence of interests between business lawyers, seeking to reposition themselves as international statesmen and philanthropists, and professors of international law, at the time a marginalized position at law faculties, who sought to gain more diplomatic traction (Sacriste and Vauchez 2007).

kp.k: Cosmopolitan capital can preserve elite privilege
kp.d: The authors contend that internationalization often raises entry barriers to prestigious expertise markets and connects to family-based elite reproduction. They associate elites’ turn toward international markets with increased competition and growth in law graduates over the preceding half century. Their arbitration research highlights co-optation and social capital rather than exclusively merit-based access; they contrast this emphasis with Seabrooke’s epistemic arbitrage framework.
qs: In many cases, strategies of internationalization serve to raise barriers of entrance to international markets of professional expertise
Very often, access to key positions within the great international legal institutions is not simply a question of legal merits or administrative procedures.

kp.k: State power structures national and transnational legal fields
kp.d: The chapter treats the state as central to the historical formation and differentiation of legal fields, rather than as external context. The authors argue that colonialism and hegemonic struggles, including the Cold War, also structure transnational legal practice. Their account connects contemporary lawyers’ governance power to long-standing incorporation into national fields of power.
qs: the state is key to understanding both the genesis, structuration and differentiation of the national legal fields

it plays a fundamental role in the structuration of transnational spaces of legal practice which very often are inscribed in longer processes of colonialism and hegemonic battles like the Cold War (Dezalay and Garth 2010, Madsen 2010).

kp.k: Legal fields enable conversion between different power resources
kp.d: The authors conceptualize legal fields as crossroads where elite lawyers simultaneously mobilize legal knowledge, social connections and political or state resources. Roles as advisers, legislators, politicians and senior officials allow alliances beyond law, making nonlegal resources consequential for transnational professional projects.
qs: the opposing strategies and alliances between different fractions of legal professionals is played out simultaneously in terms of legal capital, social capital, and political or state resources that groups are able to mobilize.

These various roles with respect to law allow for the construction of alliances beyond law and thereby a valorisation of capitals that are not strictly speaking legal but nevertheless often decisive for the furthering of transnational professional projects.

kp.k: Legal training combines meritocratic selection and inherited advantage
kp.d: The authors identify tensions between scholarly credentials and inherited family capital as a continuing engine of legal-field transformation. Apprenticeship and co-optation can transmit inherited advantage. Drawing on Martines, they describe how costs and cultural barriers enabled descendants of feudal families to capture emerging legal education; legal professionalization could therefore renew and legitimize existing hierarchies rather than simply displace them.
qs: The contradictions tied to this double logic of reproduction of legal capital – through scholarly paths that are more or less selective and meritocratic, but also through inherited capital transmitted through family lineage (including through the mechanism of the biases built into processes of apprenticeship or co-optation) –
Martines also explains the cost and the cultural barriers which reserved access to the new law faculties to the descendants of old feudal lines, who gained control of this law and justice.

kp.k: Elite sponsorship helps sustain professional autonomy
kp.d: The historical argument presents an apparent paradox: ruling groups support institutions of legal learning to recruit collaborators and successors, while those learned institutions also underpin professional autonomy. Drawing on Berman and Martines, the chapter characterizes legal development as hybridization between traditional authority, learned legitimacy and delegated state power.
qs: The ruling elite, the churches, the state, and multinationals have always sustained and financed faculties of government in order to be able to select and educate their collaborators and successors.
This way, paradoxically, their grip on politics – or the world of business – is built in part on the learned processes upon which the autonomy of this professional field resides.

kp.k: Cross-border mobility reconciles autonomy with service to power
kp.d: Using European legal history, the authors argue that elite jurists accumulated cosmopolitan resources through travel, universities and service across political and religious institutions. Mobility enabled them to serve rulers while retaining opportunities to leave patrons who threatened their credibility. They explicitly frame the continuing importance of the selective international-courtier role as a hypothesis, illustrated by European Community legal development.
qs: Our hypothesis is that the role of international courtier is not just a key to the genesis of states, but that it continues to play a vital role that is still restricted to an influential and selective fraction of the legal elite.
the clerks of the law affirm their autonomy with respect to power at the same time as they put their expertise in the service of power.

kp.k: Professional competition extends beyond knowledge and jurisdiction
kp.d: The authors accept that professional competition involves epistemic competition and jurisdictional battles, but argue that these are insufficient explanations. Creating new expertise, categories and institutions also concerns control of markets and reproduction of national elites. Their criticism of Abbott-inspired sociology and their qualification of epistemic arbitrage concern the broader social structures necessary to explain professional competition.
qs: Our basic contention is that these processes of professional competition are not simply battles over professional control; they are also part of more general processes of for example elite reproduction of national legal fields and beyond.
They are, so to say, a prolongation of national battles over domination and reproduction of elites.

kp.k: Reflexivity challenges professional categories and researchers’ assumptions
kp.d: The chapter recommends a Bourdieusian ‘double rupture’: critically examining both the construction of the research object and the academic traditions and assumptions used to explain it. For law and state formation, this requires historicizing both the object and scholarly accounts of it. Reflexivity is presented as continuous scrutiny, not a one-time methodological step.
qs: Reflexivity thus implies two very closely related actions: first, a critical reflection on the preconstructions that dominate a given subject area and, second, a self-critique as the means to considering one’s own scientific and social assumptions of the subject area.
This is not an operation that is done once and for all but is instead an on-going measure for questioning findings and the way they are gathered.

kp.k: Research can inadvertently legitimize emerging legal practices
kp.d: The authors warn that legal entrepreneurs use academic resources to legitimate their activities, potentially recruiting sociological research into those strategies. Human rights provides their example: where legal and political boundaries remain vague, scholarly discourse can confer legitimacy on weakly institutionalized practices. They regard convergence between activist research agendas and actors’ political agendas as a problem for their stated goal of scientific autonomy.
qs: many of the entrepreneurs of legal globalisation rely on academic and quasi-academic resources for legitimising their practices.
the sociologist of law, when seen from the point of view of the agents, provides a perfect object for legitimising weakly institutionalised or legalised practices.

kp.k: Comparative fieldwork exposes alliances behind official categories
kp.d: The proposed research strategy follows actors across national and international settings while independently reframing their accounts. Interviewing opposing camps and tracing multiple affiliations, bonds and antagonisms helps researchers move beyond institutional self-descriptions. The authors argue that emerging expertise develops at disciplinary boundaries, requiring inquiry into how apparently settled professional categories were produced through conflict.
qs: the researcher can interview the opposing camps, if not at the same time then immediately after each other, following a research logic that breaks with the logic of the practices of the respective agents.

Notwithstanding the way in which legal expertise is by definition presented as highly differentiated knowledge, its transformation takes place in the margin of official categories or on the frontiers of disciplines.

kp.k: Collective trajectories connect individual practices and structural change
kp.d: The authors describe their qualitative relational-biographic method: compare many actors’ trajectories to reconstruct changing networks, competencies, capital and positions within a field. This examines both actors’ influence on field formation and structural constraints on their practices. They expressly reject reliance on isolated biographies; the chapter offers a methodological synthesis of earlier studies rather than reporting a new quantified sample.
qs: we have applied a relational biographic method as a measure for comparing elements of individual trajectories with the aim of bridging them in terms of a field.
However, the method performs not by individual cases but by assembling a cumulative story that can be established by comparing a high number of trajectories within a particular field.

By interviewing the agents about their personal trajectories rather than their legal or political involvement, the researcher can assess how they pursue multiple strategies, even if they often prefer presenting themselves as associated only with a particular stance.
